standing_assumptions: Setting. The work is a textbook: Aronow and Miller, Foundations of Agnostic Statistics (Cambridge University Press, 2019). Every statement is about random variables on a probability space; Part II adds i.i.d. sampling; Part III adds the missing-data and potential-outcomes models. Locations give the printed page and the one-based page of main.pdf (316 pp.; in the body, PDF page = printed page + 18). Statements were transcribed from the page images (the 110 dpi staged renders, with higher-resolution renders of the same PDF pages where subscripts were small) and compared with the text layer for wording. (S1) Probability space. [Definition 1.1.1, p. 6 (PDF p. 24)] A set $S$ of subsets of $\Omega$ is an event space if it satisfies the following: Nonempty: $S \ne \emptyset$. Closed under complements: if $A \in S$, then $A^C \in S$. Closed under countable unions: if $A_1, A_2, A_3, ... \in S$, then $A_1 \cup A_2 \cup A_3 \cup ... \in S$. [Definition 1.1.2, p. 7 (PDF p. 25)] Kolmogorov Axioms. Let $\Omega$ be a sample space, $S$ be an event space, and $P$ be a probability measure. Then $(\Omega, S, P)$ is a probability space if it satisfies the following: Non-negativity: $\forall A \in S$, $P(A) \ge 0$, where $P(A)$ is finite and real. Unitarity: $P(\Omega) = 1$. Countable additivity: if $A_1, A_2, A_3, ... \in S$ are pairwise disjoint, then $P(A_1 \cup A_2 \cup A_3 \cup ...) = P(A_1) + P(A_2) + P(A_3) + ... = \sum_i P(A_i)$. [Footnote 11, p. 8 (PDF p. 26)] This assumption [that $(\Omega, S, P)$ is a probability space] shall henceforth be implicit in all definitions and theorems referring to $\Omega$, $S$, and/or $P$. (S2) Random variables and their distributions. [Definition 1.2.1, p. 16 (PDF p. 34)] A random variable is a function $X : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ such that, $\forall r \in \mathbb{R}$, $\{\omega \in \Omega : X(\omega) \le r\} \in S$. [Definition 1.2.2, p. 16] Let $g : U \to \mathbb{R}$ be a function, where $X(\Omega) \subseteq U \subseteq \mathbb{R}$. Then, if $g \circ X : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ is a random variable, we say that $g$ is a function of $X$, and write $g(X)$ to denote the random variable $g \circ X$. [p. 17 (PDF p. 35)] we use $\Pr[\cdot]$ to denote the probability that some condition(s) on a random variable will hold, or, equivalently, the probability that the event defined by those conditions will occur. [Definition 1.2.4, p. 18 (PDF p. 36)] A random variable $X$ is discrete if its range, $X(\Omega)$, is a countable set. [Definition 1.2.5, p. 18] For a discrete random variable $X$, the probability mass function of $X$ is $f(x) = \Pr[X = x]$, $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$. [Definition 1.2.11, p. 21 (PDF p. 39)] For a random variable $X$, the cumulative distribution function of $X$ is $F(x) = \Pr[X \le x]$, $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$. [Definition 1.2.14, p. 24 (PDF p. 42)] A random variable $X$ is continuous if there exists a non-negative function $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ such that the CDF of $X$ is $F(x) = \Pr[X \le x] = \int_{-\infty}^{x} f(u)du$, $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$. The function $f$ is called the probability density function (PDF). [Definition 1.2.15, p. 25 (PDF p. 43), as printed; see finding P001-C01-E002] For a continuous random variable $X$ with CDF $F$, the probability density function of $X$ is $f(x) = \left.\frac{dF(u)}{du}\right|_{u=x}$, $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$. [Definition 1.2.20, p. 31 (PDF p. 49)] For a random variable $X$ with PMF/PDF $f$, the support of $X$ is $\mathrm{Supp}[X] = \{x \in \mathbb{R} : f(x) > 0\}$. [Definition 1.3.1, p. 31] Let $X$ and $Y$ be random variables. Then $X = Y$ if, $\forall\omega \in \Omega$, $X(\omega) = Y(\omega)$. [Definition 1.3.16, p. 38 (PDF p. 56)] Let $X$ and $Y$ be either two discrete random variables with joint PMF $f$ or two jointly continuous random variables with joint PDF $f$. Then $X$ and $Y$ are independent if, $\forall x, y \in \mathbb{R}$, $f(x, y) = f_X(x)f_Y(y)$. We write $X \perp\!\!\!\perp Y$. [Definition 1.4.1, p. 39 (PDF p. 57)] A random vector (of length $K$) is a function $\mathbf{X} : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}^K$ such that, $\forall\omega \in \Omega$, $\mathbf{X}(\omega) = (X_{[1]}(\omega), X_{[2]}(\omega), ..., X_{[K]}(\omega))$, where $\forall k \in \{1, 2, ..., K\}$, $X_{[k]}$ is a random variable. (S3) Expectations. [Definition 2.1.1, p. 45 (PDF p. 63)] For a discrete random variable $X$ with probability mass function (PMF) $f$, if $\sum_x |x|f(x) < \infty$, then the expected value of $X$ is $\mathrm{E}[X] = \sum_x xf(x)$. For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function (PDF) $f$, if $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} |x|f(x)dx < \infty$, then the expected value of $X$ is $\mathrm{E}[X] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} xf(x)dx$. [Footnote 2, p. 45] This regularity condition (and the corresponding one in the continuous case) is known as absolute convergence. It is virtually always satisfied in practice, so we omit this technical condition from all subsequent discussion of expectations. [Footnote 3, p. 49 (PDF p. 67)] This theorem, and every subsequent theorem that we only prove for these two cases [two discrete random variables with joint PMF, or two jointly continuous random variables with joint PDF], also holds when one random variable is discrete and the other continuous. [Definition 2.1.12, p. 52 (PDF p. 70)] The variance of a random variable $X$ is $\mathrm{V}[X] = \mathrm{E}[(X - \mathrm{E}[X])^2]$. [Definition 2.1.15, p. 53 (PDF p. 71)] The standard deviation of a random variable $X$ is $\sigma[X] = \sqrt{\mathrm{V}[X]}$. [Definition 2.1.22, p. 57 (PDF p. 75)] For a random variable $X$ and $c \in \mathbb{R}$, the mean squared error of $X$ about $c$ is $\mathrm{E}[(X - c)^2]$. [Definition 2.2.1, p. 59 (PDF p. 77)] The covariance of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ is $\mathrm{Cov}[X, Y] = \mathrm{E}[(X - \mathrm{E}[X])(Y - \mathrm{E}[Y])]$. [Definition 2.2.5, p. 62 (PDF p. 80)] The correlation of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ with $\sigma[X] > 0$ and $\sigma[Y] > 0$ is $\rho[X, Y] = \frac{\mathrm{Cov}[X, Y]}{\sigma[X]\sigma[Y]}$. [Definition 2.2.10, p. 67 (PDF p. 85)] For discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ with joint PMF $f$, the conditional expectation of $Y$ given $X = x$ is $\mathrm{E}[Y|X = x] = \sum_y yf_{Y|X}(y|x)$, $\forall x \in \mathrm{Supp}[X]$. For jointly continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ with joint PDF $f$, the conditional expectation of $Y$ given $X = x$ is $\mathrm{E}[Y|X = x] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} yf_{Y|X}(y|x)dy$, $\forall x \in \mathrm{Supp}[X]$. [Definition 2.2.12, p. 68 (PDF p. 86)] For random variables $X$ and $Y$, the conditional variance of $Y$ given $X = x$ is $\mathrm{V}[Y|X = x] = \mathrm{E}[(Y - \mathrm{E}[Y|X = x])^2|X = x]$, $\forall x \in \mathrm{Supp}[X]$. [Definition 2.2.15, p. 69 (PDF p. 87)] For random variables $X$ and $Y$ with joint PMF/PDF $f$, the conditional expectation function of $Y$ given $X = x$ is $G_Y(x) = \mathrm{E}[Y|X = x]$, $\forall x \in \mathrm{Supp}[X]$. [p. 70 (PDF p. 88)] We write $\mathrm{E}[Y|X]$ to denote $G_Y(X)$; the conditional variance function is $H_Y(x) = \mathrm{V}[Y|X = x]$, and $\mathrm{V}[Y|X]$ denotes the random variable $H_Y(X)$. [Footnote 14, p. 70] Ignoring some unimportant measure-theoretic regularity conditions, namely $X(\Omega) = \mathrm{Supp}[X]$. The multivariate versions are Definitions 2.3.3 and 2.3.4 (p. 85, PDF p. 103) and the multivariate BLP, Definition 2.3.6 (p. 86, PDF p. 104; transcribed in the targets that use it). (S4) Sampling and asymptotics. [Definition 3.1.1, p. 92 (PDF p. 110)] Let $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$ be random variables with CDFs $F_1, F_2, ..., F_n$, respectively. Let $F_A$ denote the joint CDF of the random variables with indices in the set $A$. Then $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$ are independent and identically distributed if they satisfy the following: Mutually independent: $\forall A \subseteq \{1, 2, ..., n\}$, $\forall(x_1, x_2, ..., x_n) \in \mathbb{R}^n$, $F_A((x_i)_{i \in A}) = \prod_{i \in A} F_i(x_i)$. Identically distributed: $\forall i, j \in \{1, 2, ..., n\}$ and $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$, $F_i(x) = F_j(x)$. [p. 92] When we have i.i.d. random variables $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$, we use the unsubscripted letter $X$ to denote the random variable whose distribution the i.i.d. draws all share. So, for example, $\mathrm{E}[X]$ denotes the expected value common to $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$, that is, $\mathrm{E}[X] = \mathrm{E}[X_1] = \mathrm{E}[X_2] = ... = \mathrm{E}[X_n]$. [Definition 3.2.1, p. 96 (PDF p. 114)] For i.i.d. random variables $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$, a sample statistic is a function of $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$: $T_{(n)} = h_{(n)}(X_1, X_2, ..., X_n)$, where $h_{(n)} : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$, $\forall n \in \mathbb{N}$. [Definition 3.2.2, p. 97 (PDF p. 115)] For i.i.d. random variables $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$, the sample mean is $\overline{X} = \frac{X_1 + X_2 + ... + X_n}{n} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} X_i$. [Definition 3.2.6, p. 99 (PDF p. 117)] Let $(T_{(1)}, T_{(2)}, T_{(3)}, ...)$ be a sequence of random variables and let $c \in \mathbb{R}$. Then $T_{(n)}$ converges in probability to $c$ if, $\forall\epsilon > 0$, $\lim_{n \to \infty}\Pr[|T_{(n)} - c| \ge \epsilon] = 0$, or equivalently, $\lim_{n \to \infty}\Pr[|T_{(n)} - c| < \epsilon] = 1$; written $T_{(n)} \xrightarrow{p} c$. [Definition 3.2.22, p. 108 (PDF p. 126)] Let $(T_{(1)}, T_{(2)}, T_{(3)}, ...)$ be a sequence of random variables with CDFs $(F_{(1)}, F_{(2)}, F_{(3)}, ...)$, and let $T$ be a random variable with CDF $F$. Then $T_{(n)}$ converges in distribution to $T$ if, $\forall t \in \mathbb{R}$ at which $F$ is continuous, $\lim_{n \to \infty} F_{(n)}(t) = F(t)$; written $T_{(n)} \xrightarrow{d} T$. [Definition 3.2.28, p. 112 (PDF p. 130)] An estimator $\hat\theta$ is asymptotically normal if $\sqrt{n}(\hat\theta - \theta) \xrightarrow{d} N(0, \phi^2)$, for some finite $\phi > 0$. [Definition 3.3.1, p. 116 (PDF p. 134)] For i.i.d. random variables $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$, the empirical CDF $\hat F$ of $X$ is $\hat F(x) = \overline{\mathrm{I}(X \le x)}$, $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$. [Definition 3.3.2, p. 118 (PDF p. 136)] A statistical functional is a function $T : \mathcal{F} \to \mathbb{R}$, where $\mathcal{F}$ is the set of all possible CDFs. [Definition 3.3.3, p. 118] For i.i.d. random variables $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$ with common CDF $F$, the plug-in estimator of $\theta = T(F)$ is $\hat\theta = T(\hat F)$. The 'usual plug-in regularity conditions' (p. 120, PDF p. 138) are not formally defined in the book (footnote 31 names Hadamard differentiability with respect to the Kolmogorov distance and gives no formal definition). (S5) Regression. [Definition 4.1.2, pp. 146–147 (PDF pp. 164–165), with the plus sign before the last term supplied] For i.i.d. random vectors $(Y_1, \mathbf{X}_1), (Y_2, \mathbf{X}_2), ..., (Y_n, \mathbf{X}_n)$, the ordinary least squares (OLS) regression estimator is the function $\hat g(\mathbf{X}) = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1X_{[1]} + \hat\beta_2X_{[2]} + ... + \hat\beta_KX_{[K]}$ such that $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = (\hat\beta_0, \hat\beta_1, ..., \hat\beta_K) = \arg\min_{(b_0, b_1, ..., b_K) \in \mathbb{R}^{K+1}}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(Y_i - (b_0 + b_1X_{[1]i} + b_2X_{[2]i} + ... + b_KX_{[K]i})\right)^2$. We refer to $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ as the OLS coefficient estimator. [Definition 4.1.3, p. 148 (PDF p. 166)] the regressor matrix $\mathbb{X}$ is the $n \times (K + 1)$ matrix whose $i^{\mathrm{th}}$ row is $(1, X_{[1]i}, X_{[2]i}, \cdots, X_{[K]i})$. (S6) Parametric models. [Definition 5.1.1, pp. 178–179 (PDF pp. 196–197)] For a random variable $Y$ and random vector $\mathbf{X}$ of length $K$, a parametric model is a set of functions $g : \mathbb{R}^{K+1} \to \mathbb{R}$ indexed by a real-valued parameter vector $\boldsymbol\theta$ of length $\tau$: $\{g(y, \mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol\theta) : \boldsymbol\theta \in \boldsymbol\Theta\}$, where $\boldsymbol\Theta \subseteq \mathbb{R}^\tau$. The set $\boldsymbol\Theta$ is called the parameter space. The model is said to be true if $\exists\boldsymbol\theta \in \boldsymbol\Theta$ such that $f_{Y|\mathbf{X}}(y|\mathbf{x}) = g(y, \mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol\theta)$. [Definition 5.2.1, p. 186 (PDF p. 204)] the likelihood function is $\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|Y, \mathbf{X}) = g(Y, \mathbf{X}; \mathbf{t})$, and for i.i.d. observations $\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{Y}, \mathbb{X}) = \prod_{i=1}^{n}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|Y_i, \mathbf{X}_i)$. [Definition 5.2.2, pp. 186–187 (PDF pp. 204–205)] the maximum likelihood estimator of $\boldsymbol\theta$ is $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_{ML} = \arg\max_{\mathbf{t} \in \boldsymbol\Theta}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{Y}, \mathbb{X}) = \arg\max_{\mathbf{t} \in \boldsymbol\Theta}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|Y_i, \mathbf{X}_i)$. (S7) Missing data. [Definition 6.1.1, pp. 208–209 (PDF pp. 226–227)] For an outcome variable $Y_i$, the stable outcomes model is $Y_i^* = -99$ if $R_i = 0$ and $Y_i$ if $R_i = 1$; that is, $Y_i^* = Y_iR_i + (-99)(1 - R_i)$, where $Y_i^*$ is the censored version of $Y_i$ and $R_i$ is an indicator for whether $Y_i$ is observed for unit $i$. [Footnote 2, p. 208] Since we are assuming i.i.d. sampling, our inferences do not depend on the unit subscript $i$. [Definition 6.1.5, p. 213 (PDF p. 231)] $Y_i$ is missing completely at random if $Y_i \perp\!\!\!\perp R_i$ and $\Pr[R_i = 1] > 0$. [Definition 6.1.8, p. 215 (PDF p. 233)] $Y_i$ is missing at random conditional on $\mathbf{X}_i$ if $Y_i \perp\!\!\!\perp R_i|\mathbf{X}_i$ and $\exists\epsilon > 0$ such that $\Pr[R_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i] > \epsilon$. [Footnote 6, p. 215] For random variables $X$, $Y$, and $Z$ with joint PMF/PDF $f(x, y, z)$, $Y \perp\!\!\!\perp Z|X$ if, $\forall y, z \in \mathbb{R}$ and $\forall x \in \mathrm{Supp}[X]$, $f_{(Y,Z)|X}((y, z)|x) = f_{Y|X}(y|x)f_{Z|X}(z|x)$. [Definition 6.1.11, p. 217 (PDF p. 235)] the response propensity function is $p_R(\mathbf{x}) = \Pr[R_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x}]$, $\forall\mathbf{x} \in \mathrm{Supp}[\mathbf{X}_i]$. (S8) Causal inference. [Definition 7.1.1, p. 236 (PDF p. 254)] For an outcome variable $Y_i$ and binary treatment variable $D_i$, the potential outcomes model is $Y_i = Y_i(1) \cdot D_i + Y_i(0) \cdot (1 - D_i)$, where $Y_i(0)$ denotes the potential outcome under control for unit $i$, and $Y_i(1)$ denotes the potential outcome under treatment for unit $i$. [Definition 7.1.2, p. 237 (PDF p. 255)] $\tau_i = Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)$. [Definition 7.1.3, p. 238 (PDF p. 256)] the average treatment effect (ATE) is $\mathrm{E}[\tau_i]$. [Definition 7.1.9, p. 244 (PDF p. 262)] $D_i$ is randomly assigned if $(Y_i(0), Y_i(1)) \perp\!\!\!\perp D_i$ and $0 < \Pr[D_i = 1] < 1$. [Definition 7.1.12, p. 247 (PDF p. 265)] $D_i$ is strongly ignorable conditional on $\mathbf{X}_i$ if $(Y_i(0), Y_i(1)) \perp\!\!\!\perp D_i|\mathbf{X}_i$ and $\exists\epsilon > 0$ such that $\epsilon < \Pr[D_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i] < 1 - \epsilon$. [Definition 7.1.15, p. 250 (PDF p. 268)] the treatment propensity function is $p_D(\mathbf{x}) = \Pr[D_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x}]$, $\forall\mathbf{x} \in \mathrm{Supp}[\mathbf{X}_i]$. Notes for the formalizer. (a) The book works with PMFs and PDFs and states pointwise conditions ('for all $x$'); for continuous variables these hold only up to null sets (finding P001-C01-E002), so a measure-theoretic formalization should read densities and conditional expectations as versions. (b) Existence and finiteness of the expectations in a statement is a standing convention (footnote 2, p. 45). (c) Asymptotic statements are about an infinite i.i.d. sequence and $n \to \infty$. (d) In a target's statement, text in square brackets is a label or a remark of the transcriber, not the book's words.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 6.2.4, the range of the response propensity and the description of impossible estimates, corrected
canonical_claim.location: p. 225 (PDF p. 243), Section 6.2.4, first paragraph, last sentence on the page
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed sentence] We know that $\mathrm{Supp}[\mathrm{E}[R_i|\mathbf{X}_i]] \in [0, 1]$, and thus we might be concerned that a linear approximation would yield impossible propensity score estimates (predictions greater than zero or less than one). [Corrected sentence] We know that $\mathrm{Supp}[\mathrm{E}[R_i|\mathbf{X}_i]] \subseteq [0, 1]$, and thus we might be concerned that a linear approximation would yield impossible propensity score estimates (predictions greater than one or less than zero). [Formal content] Let $R_i$ be a random variable with $\mathrm{Supp}[R_i] = \{0, 1\}$ and $\mathbf{X}_i$ a random vector. Then for every $\mathbf{x} \in \mathrm{Supp}[\mathbf{X}_i]$, $\mathrm{E}[R_i|\mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x}] = \Pr[R_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x}] = p_R(\mathbf{x}) \in [0, 1]$; hence the random variable $\mathrm{E}[R_i|\mathbf{X}_i] = p_R(\mathbf{X}_i)$ takes values in $[0, 1]$, and a number $q$ is not a possible value of a propensity score if and only if $q > 1$ or $q < 0$. The printed description 'greater than zero or less than one' is satisfied by every real number, including every valid probability (for example $\frac{1}{2}$).
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: In the standing assumptions: the stable outcomes model $Y_i^* = Y_iR_i + (-99)(1 - R_i)$ with response indicator $R_i$ (Definition 6.1.1); i.i.d. sampling of units; MCAR (Definition 6.1.5); MAR conditional on $\mathbf{X}_i$ (Definition 6.1.8) and conditional independence (footnote 6, p. 215); the response propensity function $p_R$ (Definition 6.1.11); expected value, conditional expectation and the Law of Iterated Expectations (Chapter 2). [Definition 6.1.11, p. 217 (PDF p. 235)] Response Propensity Function. Suppose we observe $(R_i, \mathbf{X}_i)$, where $\mathrm{Supp}[R_i] = \{0, 1\}$. Then the response propensity function is $p_R(\mathbf{x}) = \Pr[R_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x}]$, $\forall\mathbf{x} \in \mathrm{Supp}[\mathbf{X}_i]$. The random variable $p_R(\mathbf{X}_i)$ is known as the propensity score for unit $i$. [p. 225] Recall from Definition 6.1.11 that the propensity score $p_R(\mathbf{x}) = \Pr[R_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x}]$, and, from Example 2.1.3, that $\Pr[R_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x}] = \mathrm{E}[R_i|\mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x}]$.
canonical_claim.note: Error rated Minor (kind: typo): an element sign is printed for a subset sign, and the two thresholds are interchanged in the parenthesis; the meaning (a probability lies in $[0, 1]$, a linear fit may leave it) is plain.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Theorem 6.2.6 (Reweighting under MAR), with its hypothesis corrected ('$Y_i$ is MAR conditional on $\mathbf{X}_i$')
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed statement] Theorem 6.2.6. Reweighting under MAR. Let $Y_i$ and $R_i$ be random variables with $\mathrm{Supp}[R_i] = \{0, 1\}$. Let $Y_i^* = Y_iR_i + (-99)(1 - R_i)$ and let $\mathbf{X}_i$ be a random vector. Then, if $R_i$ is MAR conditional on $\mathbf{X}_i$, $\mathrm{E}[Y_i] = \mathrm{E}\left[\frac{Y_i^*R_i}{p_R(\mathbf{X}_i)}\right]$. [Corrected statement] Theorem 6.2.6. Reweighting under MAR. Let $Y_i$ and $R_i$ be random variables with $\mathrm{Supp}[R_i] = \{0, 1\}$. Let $Y_i^* = Y_iR_i + (-99)(1 - R_i)$ and let $\mathbf{X}_i$ be a random vector. Then, if $Y_i$ is MAR conditional on $\mathbf{X}_i$, $\mathrm{E}[Y_i] = \mathrm{E}\left[\frac{Y_i^*R_i}{p_R(\mathbf{X}_i)}\right]$. [Proof, pp. 226–227, as printed] By definition, $\mathrm{E}\left[\frac{Y_i^*R_i}{p_R(\mathbf{X}_i)}\middle|\mathbf{X}_i\right] = \mathrm{E}\left[Y_i^* \cdot \frac{R_i}{\Pr[R_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i]}\middle|\mathbf{X}_i\right]$, and by stable outcomes this equals $\mathrm{E}\left[Y_i \cdot \frac{R_i}{\Pr[R_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i]}\middle|\mathbf{X}_i\right]$. Then, since MAR holds, $Y_i \perp\!\!\!\perp R_i|\mathbf{X}_i$, so this equals $\mathrm{E}[Y_i|\mathbf{X}_i] \cdot \mathrm{E}\left[\frac{R_i}{\Pr[R_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i]}\middle|\mathbf{X}_i\right] = \mathrm{E}[Y_i|\mathbf{X}_i] \cdot \frac{\mathrm{E}[R_i|\mathbf{X}_i]}{\Pr[R_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i]} = \mathrm{E}[Y_i|\mathbf{X}_i] \cdot \frac{\Pr[R_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i]}{\Pr[R_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i]} = \mathrm{E}[Y_i|\mathbf{X}_i]$. So, by the Law of Iterated Expectations, $\mathrm{E}[Y_i] = \mathrm{E}[\mathrm{E}[Y_i|\mathbf{X}_i]] = \mathrm{E}\left[\mathrm{E}\left[\frac{Y_i^*R_i}{p_R(\mathbf{X}_i)}\middle|\mathbf{X}_i\right]\right] = \mathrm{E}\left[\frac{Y_iR_i}{p_R(\mathbf{X}_i)}\right]$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: In the standing assumptions: the stable outcomes model $Y_i^* = Y_iR_i + (-99)(1 - R_i)$ with response indicator $R_i$ (Definition 6.1.1); i.i.d. sampling of units; MCAR (Definition 6.1.5); MAR conditional on $\mathbf{X}_i$ (Definition 6.1.8) and conditional independence (footnote 6, p. 215); the response propensity function $p_R$ (Definition 6.1.11); expected value, conditional expectation and the Law of Iterated Expectations (Chapter 2). [Definition 6.1.1, pp. 208–209 (PDF pp. 226–227)] Stable Outcomes Model. For an outcome variable $Y_i$, the stable outcomes model is $Y_i^* = -99$ if $R_i = 0$ and $Y_i$ if $R_i = 1$; that is, $Y_i^* = Y_iR_i + (-99)(1 - R_i)$, where $Y_i^*$ is the censored version of $Y_i$ and $R_i$ is an indicator for whether $Y_i$ is observed for unit $i$. [Definition 6.1.8, p. 215 (PDF p. 233)] Missing at Random (MAR). Let $Y_i$ and $R_i$ be random variables with $\mathrm{Supp}[R_i] = \{0, 1\}$, let $Y_i^* = Y_iR_i + (-99)(1 - R_i)$, and let $\mathbf{X}_i$ be a random vector. Then $Y_i$ is missing at random conditional on $\mathbf{X}_i$ if the following conditions hold: $Y_i \perp\!\!\!\perp R_i|\mathbf{X}_i$ (independence of outcome and response conditional on $\mathbf{X}_i$); $\exists\epsilon > 0$ such that $\Pr[R_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i] > \epsilon$ (nonzero probability of response conditional on $\mathbf{X}_i$). [Footnote 6] For random variables $X$, $Y$, and $Z$ with joint PMF/PDF $f(x, y, z)$, $Y \perp\!\!\!\perp Z|X$ if, $\forall y, z \in \mathbb{R}$ and $\forall x \in \mathrm{Supp}[X]$, $f_{(Y,Z)|X}((y, z)|x) = f_{Y|X}(y|x)f_{Z|X}(z|x)$. If $Y \perp\!\!\!\perp Z|X$, all the implications of independence derived in Chapters 1 and 2 hold conditional on $X$; for example, $\mathrm{E}[Y|X] = \mathrm{E}[Y|Z, X]$. [Footnote 7] The statement that $\Pr[R_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i] > \epsilon$ is equivalent to $\forall\mathbf{x} \in \mathrm{Supp}[\mathbf{X}_i]$, $\Pr[R_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x}] > \epsilon$. [Definition 6.1.11, p. 217 (PDF p. 235)] Response Propensity Function. Suppose we observe $(R_i, \mathbf{X}_i)$, where $\mathrm{Supp}[R_i] = \{0, 1\}$. Then the response propensity function is $p_R(\mathbf{x}) = \Pr[R_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x}]$, $\forall\mathbf{x} \in \mathrm{Supp}[\mathbf{X}_i]$. The random variable $p_R(\mathbf{X}_i)$ is known as the propensity score for unit $i$.
canonical_claim.note: Error rated Minor (kind: notation): '$R_i$ is MAR' is printed for '$Y_i$ is MAR'; Definition 6.1.8 defines the property for $Y_i$, and the proof uses the intended hypothesis $Y_i \perp\!\!\!\perp R_i|\mathbf{X}_i$. The corrected theorem is the formal content of headline claim P001-ch06-H6 ($\mathrm{E}[Y_i] = \mathrm{E}[Y_i^*R_i/p_R(\mathbf{X}_i)]$ under MAR), which held up. $Y_i^*R_i = Y_iR_i$ exactly, which is why the proof ends with $Y_iR_i$. Positivity (the second MAR condition) makes the division by $p_R(\mathbf{X}_i)$ legitimate.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 6.2.5, the sentence 'In the case where there is a discrete and finite number of values for $\mathbf{X}_i$, the IPW estimator is logically equivalent to the plug-in estimator from Section 6.2.1', as printed
canonical_claim.location: p. 228 (PDF p. 246), first paragraph. Definition 6.2.7: p. 227 (PDF p. 245). Section 6.2.1 plug-in estimator: p. 219 (PDF p. 237). Section 6.2.4: pp. 225–226 (PDF pp. 243–244)
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed statement] In the case where there is a discrete and finite number of values for $\mathbf{X}_i$, the IPW estimator is logically equivalent to the plug-in estimator from Section 6.2.1 (Plug-In Estimation). [What is refuted] Equality of the two sample estimators, $\hat{\mathrm{E}}_{IPW}[Y_i] = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{Y_i^*R_i}{\hat p_R(\mathbf{X}_i)}$ (Definition 6.2.7) and the post-stratification plug-in estimator of Section 6.2.1, whenever $\mathbf{X}_i$ has finitely many values, with $\hat p_R$ the ML plug-in estimate from a binary choice model that Section 6.2.4 adopts ('Regardless of the exact specification, we will assume as we proceed that we are using an ML plug-in estimate from a binary choice model'). Equality when $\hat p_R$ is the observed response rate in each cell is not refuted. [Counterexample, from the validator] Twelve units with $\mathbf{X}_i = (1, x_i)$: units 1–4 have $x_i = -1$, units 5–8 have $x_i = 0$, units 9–12 have $x_i = 1$. Responses $R_i = 1, 1, 0, 0;\ 1, 1, 1, 0;\ 1, 1, 0, 0$. Observed outcomes of the respondents: $Y_1 = \frac{1}{4}$, $Y_2 = \frac{1}{2}$; $Y_5 = \frac{1}{4}$, $Y_6 = \frac{1}{2}$, $Y_7 = \frac{3}{4}$; $Y_9 = \frac{1}{4}$, $Y_{10} = \frac{1}{2}$. Then: (a) the logit model $h(\mathbf{X}_i\boldsymbol\beta) = \frac{e^{\beta_0 + \beta_1x_i}}{1 + e^{\beta_0 + \beta_1x_i}}$ has the unique ML estimate $(\hat\beta_0, \hat\beta_1) = (\log\frac{7}{5}, 0)$, so $\hat p_R(\mathbf{X}_i) = \frac{7}{12}$ for every unit; (b) $\hat{\mathrm{E}}_{IPW}[Y_i] = \frac{1}{12} \cdot \frac{12}{7}\left(\frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{2} + \frac{3}{4} + \frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{2}\right) = \frac{3}{7}$; (c) the plug-in estimator of Section 6.2.1 is $\frac{3}{8} \cdot \frac{4}{12} + \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{4}{12} + \frac{3}{8} \cdot \frac{4}{12} = \frac{5}{12}$; (d) $\frac{3}{7} - \frac{5}{12} = \frac{1}{84} \ne 0$. Every cell contains respondents and nonrespondents.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: In the standing assumptions: the stable outcomes model $Y_i^* = Y_iR_i + (-99)(1 - R_i)$ with response indicator $R_i$ (Definition 6.1.1); i.i.d. sampling of units; MCAR (Definition 6.1.5); MAR conditional on $\mathbf{X}_i$ (Definition 6.1.8) and conditional independence (footnote 6, p. 215); the response propensity function $p_R$ (Definition 6.1.11); expected value, conditional expectation and the Law of Iterated Expectations (Chapter 2). [Definition 6.1.1, pp. 208–209 (PDF pp. 226–227)] Stable Outcomes Model. For an outcome variable $Y_i$, the stable outcomes model is $Y_i^* = -99$ if $R_i = 0$ and $Y_i$ if $R_i = 1$; that is, $Y_i^* = Y_iR_i + (-99)(1 - R_i)$, where $Y_i^*$ is the censored version of $Y_i$ and $R_i$ is an indicator for whether $Y_i$ is observed for unit $i$. [Section 6.2.1, p. 219] $\hat{\mathrm{E}}[Y_i] = \sum_{\mathbf{x} \in \widehat{\mathrm{Supp}}[\mathbf{X}_i]}\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} Y_i^*R_i \cdot \mathrm{I}(\mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x})}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} R_i \cdot \mathrm{I}(\mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x})} \cdot \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathrm{I}(\mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x})}{n}$. [Definition 6.2.7, p. 227] Given $n$ i.i.d. observations of $(Y_i^*, R_i, \mathbf{X}_i)$, the inverse probability–weighted estimator for $\mathrm{E}[Y_i]$ is $\hat{\mathrm{E}}_{IPW}[Y_i] = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{Y_i^*R_i}{\hat p_R(\mathbf{X}_i)}$. [Section 6.2.4, p. 226] ML propensity score estimates from a binary choice model with mean function $h$: $\hat p_R(\mathbf{X}_i) = h(\mathbf{X}_i\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{ML})$. [Definition 5.1.9, p. 183 (PDF p. 201)] the logit mean function $h(u) = \frac{e^u}{1 + e^u}$.
canonical_claim.note: Error rated Minor: a one-sentence aside about intuition; both estimators keep the same target and their own consistency conditions, and no theorem or reported number uses the equality. The ML fit in (a): the score equations are $\sum_i(R_i - \hat p_i) = 0$ and $\sum_i x_i(R_i - \hat p_i) = 0$; the response counts by cell are $2, 3, 2$ out of 4, so by symmetry the slope is 0 and the common fitted probability is $\frac{7}{12}$; uniqueness follows from strict concavity of the logit log-likelihood with a full-rank design. The validator shows the sample has positive probability under an i.i.d. MAR population with a correctly specified logit model, and that known true probabilities give the same kind of discrepancy.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 6.2.5, equivalence of the IPW estimator and the post-stratification plug-in estimator, corrected: it holds when the estimated response probability in each cell is the observed respondent fraction
canonical_claim.statement: [Corrected sentence] When the covariates have finite discrete support, every observed covariate cell has at least one respondent, and the estimated response probability in each cell is its observed respondent fraction, the IPW estimator equals the plug-in estimator from Section 6.2.1 (Plug-In Estimation). [In full] Let $(Y_i^*, R_i, \mathbf{X}_i)_{i=1}^{n}$ be a sample, let $\mathcal{C}$ be the finite set of observed values of $\mathbf{X}_i$, and for $\mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{C}$ let $n_{\mathbf{x}} = \sum_i\mathrm{I}(\mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x})$, $r_{\mathbf{x}} = \sum_i R_i\mathrm{I}(\mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x})$ and $S_{\mathbf{x}} = \sum_i Y_i^*R_i\mathrm{I}(\mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x})$, with $r_{\mathbf{x}} > 0$ for all $\mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{C}$. Let $q_{\mathbf{x}} = \hat p_R(\mathbf{x}) > 0$ be the fitted probability in cell $\mathbf{x}$. Then (i) $\hat{\mathrm{E}}_{IPW}[Y_i] = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{\mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{C}}\frac{S_{\mathbf{x}}}{q_{\mathbf{x}}}$ and the plug-in estimator of Section 6.2.1 equals $\frac{1}{n}\sum_{\mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{C}}\frac{n_{\mathbf{x}}S_{\mathbf{x}}}{r_{\mathbf{x}}}$, so $\hat{\mathrm{E}}_{IPW}[Y_i] - \hat{\mathrm{E}}[Y_i] = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{\mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{C}} S_{\mathbf{x}}\left(\frac{1}{q_{\mathbf{x}}} - \frac{n_{\mathbf{x}}}{r_{\mathbf{x}}}\right)$; (ii) if $q_{\mathbf{x}} = r_{\mathbf{x}}/n_{\mathbf{x}}$ for every $\mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{C}$, the two estimators are equal; (iii) for fixed covariates, responses and fitted probabilities, the two estimators are equal for all outcome vectors if and only if $q_{\mathbf{x}} = r_{\mathbf{x}}/n_{\mathbf{x}}$ for every $\mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{C}$; (iv) with $q_{\mathbf{x}} = r_{\mathbf{x}}/n_{\mathbf{x}}$, the denominator of the stabilized IPW estimator is $\frac{1}{n}\sum_i\frac{R_i}{\hat p_R(\mathbf{X}_i)} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{\mathbf{x}} n_{\mathbf{x}} = 1$, so the stabilized IPW estimator (Definition 6.2.8) equals both.

canonical_claim.note: Error rated Minor. The corrected statement is an exact algebraic identity for each sample. The 'only if' in (iii) is about equality as an identity in the outcomes; for one particular outcome vector other fitted probabilities can give equality by cancellation, as the validator notes. The observed cell fractions are the ML estimates under a saturated Bernoulli model. Headline claim P001-ch06-H6 includes this equivalence and holds with the qualification.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: The paragraph after Definition 6.2.8 (Stabilized IPW Estimator for Missing Data): the sum whose between-sample variation the stabilized estimator accounts for, corrected ($R_i$ in the numerator)
canonical_claim.location: p. 228 (PDF p. 246), Definition 6.2.8 and the paragraph after it
canonical_claim.statement: [Definition 6.2.8, as printed; unchanged] Stabilized IPW Estimator for Missing Data. Let $Y_i$ and $R_i$ be random variables with $\mathrm{Supp}[R_i] = \{0, 1\}$. Let $Y_i^* = Y_iR_i + (-99)(1 - R_i)$ and let $\mathbf{X}_i$ be a random vector. Then, given $n$ i.i.d. observations of $(Y_i^*, R_i, \mathbf{X}_i)$, the stabilized IPW estimator for $\mathrm{E}[Y_i]$ is $\hat{\mathrm{E}}_{SIPW}[Y_i] = \frac{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{Y_iR_i}{\hat p_R(\mathbf{X}_i)}}{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{R_i}{\hat p_R(\mathbf{X}_i)}}$. [Printed passage] When $\hat p_R(\mathbf{X}_i)$ converges (in an appropriate functional sense) to $p_R(\mathbf{X}_i)$, then the denominator of the fraction will converge in probability to 1. To see this, note that with the true propensity score, $\mathrm{E}\left[\frac{R_i}{p_R(\mathbf{X}_i)}\right] = 1$. ... Because the stabilized IPW estimator accounts for this between-sample variation in $\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{p_R(\mathbf{X}_i)}$, it typically confers efficiency gains over the IPW estimator in practice. [Corrected sum] ... this between-sample variation in $\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{R_i}{p_R(\mathbf{X}_i)}$ ... [Formal content] Let $R_i$ have $\mathrm{Supp}[R_i] = \{0, 1\}$ and let $p_R(\mathbf{X}_i) = \Pr[R_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i] > \epsilon > 0$. Then (i) $\mathrm{E}\left[\frac{R_i}{p_R(\mathbf{X}_i)}\middle|\mathbf{X}_i\right] = 1$ and $\mathrm{E}\left[\frac{R_i}{p_R(\mathbf{X}_i)}\right] = 1$, so for i.i.d. units $\mathrm{E}\left[\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{R_i}{p_R(\mathbf{X}_i)}\right] = 1$ for every $n$; (ii) $\mathrm{E}\left[\frac{1}{p_R(\mathbf{X}_i)}\right] \ge 1$, with equality if and only if $p_R(\mathbf{X}_i) = 1$ with probability one; so the all-unit sum $\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{p_R(\mathbf{X}_i)}$ is not the denominator of Definition 6.2.8 and does not have expectation 1 unless response is certain.
